author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein
text: An algorithm is any well-defined computational procedure that takes some value, or set of values, as input and produces some value, or set of values, as output. An algorithm is thus a sequence of computational steps that transform the input into the output. We can also view an algorithm as a tool for solving a well-specified computational problem.

author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein
text: view an algorithm as a tool for solving a well-specified computational problem. The divide-and-conquer design paradigm involves three steps at each level of recursion: Divide the problem into a number of subproblems that are smaller instances of the same problem. Conquer the subproblems by solving them recursively. If the subproblem sizes are small enough, however, just solve the subproblems in a straightforward manner.

author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein
text: e small enough, however, just solve the subproblems in a straightforward manner. Combine the solutions to the subproblems into the solution for the original problem. Dynamic programming solves problems by combining the solutions to subproblems. Dynamic programming typically applies to optimization problems in which we make a set of choices in order to arrive at an optimal solution.

author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, Clifford Stein
text: ems in which we make a set of choices in order to arrive at an optimal solution. It requires two key ingredients: optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution contains within it optimal solutions to subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning a recursive algorithm visits the same subproblems repeatedly rather than generating new subproblems.

author: Abraham Silberschatz, Peter B. Galvin
text: A process is a program in execution. A process execution must progress in sequential fashion. A process is more than the program code, which is sometimes known as the text section. It also includes the current activity, as represented by the value of the program counter and the contents of the processor registers. Process scheduling selects among available processes for the next execution on the CPU core.

Detailed System Architecture DocMind is designed as an end-to-end document intelligence system that enables users to interact with their uploaded documents through natural-language queries. The system follows a Retrieval-Augmented Generation architecture in which relevant information is retrieved from the indexed document collection before being provided to a Large Language Model (LLM) for response generation.

author: Gaurav
text: n before being provided to a Large Language Model (LLM) for response generation. The complete workflow consists of the following stages: Document Upload → Text Extraction → Preprocessing → Text Chunking → Embedding Generation → Vector Database Indexing → User Query → Query Embedding → Similarity Search → Relevant Context Retrieval → RAG Prompt Construction → LLM Response Generation → Source-Referenced Response The document-processing stage prepares the uploaded content for semantic retrieval, wh

author: Gaurav
text: cument-processing stage prepares the uploaded content for semantic retrieval, while the query-processing stage retrieves the most relevant document segments and supplies them as context to the language model. S1.1 Document Processing Pipeline 1 Document Upload: The user uploads a supported document through the DocMind web interface. 2 Text Extraction: Text is extracted from the uploaded document using an appropriate document-processing library.

author: Gaurav
text: ted from the uploaded document using an appropriate document-processing library. 3 Preprocessing: Extracted text is cleaned by handling unnecessary characters, formatting noise and other irrelevant content. 4 Chunking: The processed text is divided into smaller overlapping chunks to make retrieval more effective while preserving sufficient contextual information. 5 Embedding Generation: Each document chunk is converted into a numerical vector representation using a pre-trained embedding model.

author: Gaurav
text: rted into a numerical vector representation using a pre-trained embedding model. 6 Vector Indexing: The generated vectors are stored in a vector database together with metadata such as document identifier, source and chunk information. S2. Query Processing and RAG Workflow When a user submits a natural-language question, DocMind processes the query through the following stages. Step 1 — User Query. The user enters a natural-language question related to the uploaded documents.

author: Gaurav
text: . The user enters a natural-language question related to the uploaded documents. Step 2 — Query Embedding. The question is converted into an embedding using the same or compatible embedding representation used for document chunks. Step 3 — Semantic Similarity Search. The query embedding is compared with indexed document embeddings using vector similarity search. [Page 2] 2 Step 4 — Relevant Context Retrieval.

author: Gaurav
text: using vector similarity search. [Page 2] 2 Step 4 — Relevant Context Retrieval. The highest-ranked document chunks are retrieved based on their semantic similarity to the query. Step 5 — Context Construction. The retrieved chunks are combined with the user's question to construct the context supplied to the LLM. Step 6 — Response Generation. The LLM generates an answer using the retrieved document context rather than relying exclusively on its pretrained knowledge.

author: Gaurav
text: ed document context rather than relying exclusively on its pretrained knowledge. Step 7 — Source Presentation. DocMind presents the generated response together with available document source information, allowing the user to identify the supporting document content. S3. Additional Contribution of DocMind The proposed DocMind framework integrates multiple components into a unified document intelligence workflow.

author: Gaurav
text: rk integrates multiple components into a unified document intelligence workflow. Rather than treating document retrieval, semantic search and language generation as independent tasks, the system combines document ingestion, preprocessing, semantic representation, vector retrieval, context construction and LLM-based generation into a single user-facing workflow.

author: Gaurav
text: ontext construction and LLM-based generation into a single user-facing workflow. The system further emphasizes source-grounded interaction, where retrieved document content is used as the context for response generation and associated source information is presented to the user. This design aims to improve transparency and make generated responses more traceable to the user’s document collection. S19.

Supplementary Material Summary This supplementary material provides additional evidence supporting the technical design and evaluation of DocMind. It describes the complete RAG workflow, document processing pipeline, metadata structure, semantic retrieval process, response-generation process, evaluation methodology, error categories, robustness tests and reproducibility information.
